newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Amnesty seen set to test S.African reconciliation.
newsitem.headline: Amnesty seen set to test S.African reconciliation.

text.p: South Africa's truth commission on Tuesday pardoned one of apartheid's most notorious killer policemen in a decision likely to test the limits of national reconciliation.
Former policeman Brian Mitchell, who is serving a 30-year sentence for the murder of 11 people in December 1988, was granted amnesty by Archbishop Desmond Tutu's Truth and Reconciliation Commission.
"This is the first amnesty decision in favour of a former security force member," said commission spokesman John Allen.

The truth commission's amnesty committee, headed by black judge Hassen Mall, said in a statement that Mitchell had satisfied the conditions laid down in the National Unity and Reconciliation Act for political amnesty.
University of Cape Town political scientist David Welsh said however Mitchell's pardon would test the limits of national reconciliation after more than 300 years of white minority rule.
"I think people are going to be outraged by this decision. Many people are going to say he has not expunged his debt to society," he said.

But he said the decision to release Mitchell would tip the scales in favour of former apartheid bosses advising their followers to accept the amnesty offer, which is amongst agreed terms for the transition from white rule to democracy.

"Brian Mitchell was convicted of a most horrendous massacre -- one that fills everyone with utter revulsion. If they were looking for a sweetener to induce people to come forward, then they couldn't have come up with a better case," he said.
The decision came four days before the deadline for amnesty applications to the commission charged with reconciling blacks and whites under South Africa's first democratic government.
Tutu's commission will continue for another year to unravel the history of white rule and the war against it, but applications for political amnesty must be made this week.
Members of President Nelson Mandela's African National Congress (ANC) have been slow to seek pardon for human rights crimes committed in their 30-year struggle against apartheid.
Most veterans of the ANC's guerrilla army argue that theirs was a just war and that their actions do not require pardon.

Veterans of the apartheid security forces are split on the issue, with former defence minister Magnus Malan advising his followers to boycott the commission and former police chief Johan van der Merwe urging his men to seek pardon.
In a message relayed by his lawyer, Mitchell urged former colleagues to accept the amnesty, which is offered in return for a full confession. Repentence is not a condition.
Lawyer Eugene Nation told Reuters that he expected Mitchell to be released on Wednesday from the Pietermaritzburg prison in the Zulu heartland of KwaZulu-Natal, where the massacre occured.
Mitchell admitted in testimony supporting his amnesty bid that he organised an attack on a local leader of the United Democratic Front, then the internal arm of Mandela's ANC.
The four black policemen ordered to carry out the attack went to the wrong house and instead killed 11 mourners holding an all-night vigil for a dead relative.
They were sentenced to death with Mitchell in 1992, but were pardoned in 1994 when Mitchell's sentence was commuted to 30 years' imprisonment.
